sections.heading: Coming to you as the sinner I am
sections.text: Father, you are the God who listened to the tax collector when he could only say, “Have mercy on me.” I come to you the same way. I am a sinner—not only because of what I have done, but because of what I am apart from your grace. Your Word tells me the truth about me, and I do not want to argue with it. Help me to feel the seriousness of my sin without hiding from you.
theological_themes: Honest confession of sin before God
Scripture’s truthful diagnosis of the human heart

scripture_references.connection: Jesus presents the tax collector’s simple cry for mercy as the posture of a person who goes home justified. This directly grounds the prayer’s opening plea and its refusal to come to God with self-defense.
Paul teaches that sin is universal, not merely a matter of isolated failures. This supports the prayer’s confession that sin is both personal practice and part of fallen human nature.

sections.heading: Not giving up, because your mercy is certain
sections.text: But you have not left me with despair as my only option. Your grace is not uncertain or reluctant. With you there is more redemption than there is sin in me. My sins are many, and some of them are shameful even to remember, but you have still held out mercy to me. You have given me real hope that I may come near, receive life, and not be turned away.
theological_themes: God’s grace gives hope to guilty sinners
Assurance rests on God’s promise, not on the sinner’s worthiness

scripture_references.connection: The psalm holds together the reality of guilt with confident hope in the Lord’s forgiveness and abundant redemption. It supports the prayer’s movement from conviction to hope without minimizing sin.
Because Christ is the great high priest, believers are invited to draw near to God’s throne for mercy and grace. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that God’s mercy is truly offered to the needy.

sections.heading: Running to the refuge you have opened
sections.text: Please strengthen my heart to trust you: your sufficiency, your promises, and the testimony of all the people you have rescued before me. Let me run to the shelter where sinners have found safety again and again. Wash me in the cleansing you have provided, because I cannot make myself clean.
theological_themes: Faith encouraged by God’s promises and past mercies
Cleansing from sin provided by God

scripture_references.connection: This passage describes God’s promise and oath as strong encouragement for those who flee to him for refuge. It fits the prayer’s request to be strengthened by God’s reliability and to run to the shelter he provides.
Zechariah speaks of a fountain opened for cleansing from sin and uncleanness. The prayer draws on that biblical image to ask God for cleansing that is freely provided rather than self-produced.
John connects honest confession with God’s faithfulness to forgive and cleanse through Christ. This supports the prayer’s confidence that real defilement can be truly washed away.

sections.heading: Agreeing with you about sin and holiness
sections.text: Lord, sin is not a small thing to you. It is the thing you hate, and it is what puts distance between you and me. You cannot stop being holy in order to make me comfortable. You will not make me happy with yourself while leaving me unchanged and at home in sin. So make me holy. Make me into someone you delight in, and make my heart able to delight in you.
theological_themes: God’s holiness and hatred of sin
God’s saving purpose includes making his people holy
True joy in God requires transformation

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah explains that sin creates separation between God and his people, not because God is weak but because sin is morally serious. This directly supports the prayer’s claim that sin is the barrier between the sinner and God.
Peter calls believers to holiness because God himself is holy. This grounds the prayer’s desire not merely to be pardoned, but to be made fit for fellowship with the holy God.

Hebrews treats holiness as essential to seeing the Lord, not as an optional spiritual preference. This supports the prayer’s insistence that happiness with God cannot be separated from being made holy.

sections.heading: Learning to love what you command
sections.text: Teach me to agree with your law from the inside. When your commands feel strict, do not let me accuse you of being harsh. Let me grieve over how far I fall short instead of blaming your standards. Keep me from questioning your right to command me. Help me to see that what you say is good, wise, and right.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes an inward delight in God’s law, even while honestly recognizing remaining sin. This supports the prayer’s desire to love God’s commands while mourning lack of conformity to them.
This section of Psalm 119 praises the righteousness and trustworthiness of God’s rules. It supports the prayer’s request to esteem God’s commands as right rather than resent them as oppressive.

sections.heading: Changing my actions from the inside out
sections.text: By your Spirit in me, make my obedience come from real faith and love, not from appearance or pressure. Bring my desires, habits, and attitudes into line with what you call good. Let what I do grow out of what you are making me inside.
theological_themes: Sanctification as inner and outward transformation

scripture_references.connection: God promises to give his people a new heart and put his Spirit within them so they walk in his ways. This directly grounds the prayer’s request for inward renewal that produces outward obedience.

Paul teaches that what the law could not accomplish because of human sin, God does through Christ and the Spirit, so that righteous requirement is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s longing for Spirit-formed obedience.

The fruit of the Spirit includes transformed desires and conduct, and Paul calls believers to keep in step with the Spirit. This illuminates the prayer’s request for dispositions and practices to be reshaped by God.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly states that God cannot make the sinner happy with himself until he has made the sinner holy. This could be misunderstood as denying justification by grace or present assurance, so the adaptation preserves the point as sanctification being inseparable from fellowship with a holy God, not as holiness earning acceptance.

The original’s image of the golden sceptre comes from Esther’s court scene. Because its use in the prayer is devotional and typological rather than an explicit biblical promise, the adaptation retained the idea of mercy being held out without leaning heavily on the image or citing Esther as direct doctrinal support.
significant_interpretive_choices: “There is no ‘peradventure’ in thy grace” was rendered as God’s grace being certain and not reluctant, preserving the original’s assurance that mercy rests on God’s promise rather than on anxious speculation.
“A token for good” was interpreted as God giving real hope and encouragement to come for mercy, rather than as a specific outward sign or circumstance.

“Practice spring from principle” was rendered as obedience flowing from faith and love rather than appearance or pressure, since the original contrasts inward spiritual principle with merely external duty.
